query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an FCC matrix, degradation during prolonged high‐temperature exposure is primarily governed by the selective oxidation of reactive species (e.g., Cr, Ti, and minor Al) at grain boundaries that leads to the formation of a layered, non-uniform oxide scale. The growth of this oxide layer induces a mismatch in volume and generates substantial growth stresses. Once the accumulated stress exceeds interfacial cohesion, the oxide scale spalls, rapidly exposing fresh metal to further oxidation and promoting intergranular cracking that eventually triggers catastrophic failure. Conversely, in reducing gas atmospheres, insufficient or uneven oxidation permits enhanced vacancy clustering and grain boundary weakening, also predisposing the material to abrupt mechanical failure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-fabricated Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with a fine-grained, uniform FCC matrix and minimal pre-existing oxides.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to elevated temperatures (e.g., 800°C) in controlled gas atmospheres; one set under an oxidizing environment (defined oxygen partial pressure) and another under a reducing (or inert with reducing additives) atmosphere.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure in the range of 700–1000°C with precisely controlled gas compositions – for oxidizing conditions, a controlled oxygen partial pressure (e.g., ~10 mbar) and for reducing conditions, an atmosphere enriched with reducing species (e.g., H2 diluted in an inert gas).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and evolution of a layered oxide scale—particularly at grain boundaries—and any associated precipitated oxide phases (such as Cr-rich or Ti-rich oxides) that compromise interfacial cohesion.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures in an oxidizing gas, selective oxidation preferentially occurs at grain boundaries (where local defects and high energy sites exist) producing a stratified oxide film. The mismatch in thermal expansion and growth-induced stresses between the substrate and the oxide layers leads to spallation. This spalling exposes fresh alloy surfaces, accelerating local oxidation and crack initiation. Under reducing conditions, the lack of a well-developed oxide scale allows for alternative degradation mechanisms—such as increased vacancy aggregation and diffusion-driven embrittlement—which also compromise mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxidizing conditions, a multilayer oxide structure will form along grain boundaries and eventually spall, being accompanied by microcrack formation and a marked drop in mechanical properties leading to catastrophic failure. Under reducing conditions, while a continuous protective oxide layer may not form, observable intergranular weakening (e.g., from vacancy clusters) will lead to localized embrittlement and premature failure, albeit with a distinct microstructural signature compared to the oxidizing case.
generation.baseline: The as-manufactured alloy, when maintained in an inert or mildly reactive environment at room temperature, retains its uniform FCC matrix and exhibits stable mechanical properties with no significant oxide formation or degradation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold when the alloy is exposed to temperatures between approximately 700°C and 1000°C, with systematic gas atmospheres ranging from oxidizing (e.g., controlled oxygen partial pressures) to reducing (e.g., H2-containing mixtures).
generation.uncertainty: The relative contributions of oxide-induced spallation versus diffusion-driven embrittlement under reducing conditions are not yet precisely quantified. In addition, the specific oxide compositions and their detailed growth kinetics at the nanometer scale remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several identical Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples and divide them into two groups. Expose one group to 800°C in a controlled oxidizing environment (e.g., with an oxygen partial pressure around 10 mbar) and the other group to an equivalent temperature in a reducing atmosphere (e.g., a mixture of inert gas with a small percentage of H2). Monitor the evolution of the surface and grain boundary microstructures over time using of high-resolution characterization techniques.
measurements: Microstructural analysis using TEM/SEM to detect oxide layer formation, spallation, and grain boundary changes.
Surface chemical composition via XPS or EDS to analyze oxide chemistry and thickness.
Mechanical testing (e.g., tensile or fracture toughness measurements) before and after exposure to quantify degradation.
EBSD mapping to observe any changes in grain boundary character and detect crack initiation sites.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, in the oxidizing environment, no distinct layered oxide scale forms or if there is no evidence of oxide spallation and associated intergranular cracking, or if the degradation behavior under reducing conditions is indistinguishable from that in oxidizing conditions (i.e. no distinct mechanism can be discerned), then the proposed hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 6 presents the mechanical stability analysis of the oxide scales. As shown in Figure 6, the cyclic oxidation results reveal pronounced differences in spallation resistance among the three alloys. The Base Alloy undergoes severe oxide-scale spallation after 100 thermal cycles at 1000 °C, resulting in substantial mass loss. The Synergy Alloy shows improved cyclic oxidation resistance, but measurable scale degradation still occurs. In contrast, the Innovation Alloy exhibits a mass change of only 0.05 ± 0.02 mg/cm2 after 100 cycles, with almost no detectable spallation, demonstrating excellent scale stability under thermal cycling. The simulated stress evolution further indicates that the oxide scale on the Innovation Alloy accumulates growth stress more slowly and can more effectively accommodate stress through local deformation and defect healing. Scratch testing confirms this enhanced interfacial stability: the critical load and interfacial fracture energy reach 78 N and 14.8 J/m2, respectively, which are substantially higher than those of the Synergy Alloy.
